title: The Playbook — the options strategies people and institutions actually run
lede: Page 09 is about structures — the legs. This page is about strategies: what pensions, hedge funds, dealers and retail traders actually run, why each one gets paid, and how each one blows up. It leans on almost every page in the series, and each strategy links to the pages that explain its machinery.

chapters.title: Every strategy is paid for a shape of risk
chapters.dek: Sell insurance and you earn steady premiums with a rare large loss. Buy it and you bleed steadily for a rare large gain. Same market, opposite shapes.

figures.title: Growth of $1 over 30 simulated years, log scale
figures.caption: Notice the red line: smooth for years, then a cliff. That is what selling insurance looks like, and it is why a strategy's average return says almost nothing until you have seen its worst month. Set the variance risk premium to zero and put-writing's return all but disappears while its cliffs stay.

checks.q: A put-writing fund shows 93% winning months and a steady equity curve for six years. What is the most important number you do not yet have?
checks.right: Its loss in a crash month — the strategy is paid to hold that tail, and six calm years tell you almost nothing about its size
checks.why: The tail. Negative-skew strategies look best right before they look worst. Sharpe ratios computed over calm periods flatter them, and the win rate is high by construction ( page 18 ). Ask what the fund lost in the worst month it could plausibly face, and whether it was leveraged into it.

chapters.text: Options strategies earn money for a small number of reasons, and the most important one is that somebody is paying to get rid of a risk. Pensions buy puts because a crash would breach their mandate; corporates buy collars because their board demands a floor; investors buy structured notes for a coupon and sell crash risk to get it. Whoever takes the other side collects a premium — and inherits the risk. That makes the shape of the returns the real product. The figure runs one simulated 30-year market through three strategies. Ordinary months have 15% volatility; crash months arrive about once a decade and cost a quarter of the index. Options are priced at implied volatility 25% above the ordinary months' realized — a variance risk premium in line with what index options have historically carried — and the far put is marked up again for skew. In the default history, systematic put-writing wins in 93% of months and has a skewness of −9.2 : hundreds of small gains and a few losses as large as 19% in a month. The index grows 13.0% a year with a worst drawdown of 26% . The index with a rolled tail hedge — 15%-out-of-the-money puts bought every month — grows 13.6% with a worst drawdown of 19% : in this history the hedge paid for itself in the crash months. Press "New history" a few times and watch how much that last result depends on when the crashes land. That dependence is the whole argument about tail hedging, in one button. chapters.title: The playbook
chapters.dek: Fifteen strategies people and institutions actually run. Each pays for a reason, and each has a way it fails that the people running it know about and sometimes forget.

checks.q: Why do dispersion trades, put-writing and short-VIX products tend to lose money in the same weeks?
checks.right: They are all short the same thing: the jump in volatility and correlation that defines a crash. Diversifying across them diversifies the packaging, not the risk
checks.why: Same risk, different wrappers. Each is paid a premium for bearing crash risk, so a crash collects on all of them together. A book that holds several of them is more concentrated than its strategy list suggests — page 23 's stress limits exist for exactly this.

chapters.text: Read each strategy in the same order: why it gets paid, how it is run, how it loses, and what the people who survive it do differently. The pattern repeats. Strategies that sell insurance — put-writing, overwriting, short volatility, dispersion, structured-product issuance — earn steadily and lose in crises, all at once. Strategies that buy it — tail hedging, long volatility — bleed and pay off rarely. Strategies that sell a service — market making, financing — earn a spread and lose to informed flow or plumbing. The edge in all of them comes from the five sources in page 09's field guide; the strategy is just how it is packaged.

chapters.title: Choosing a strategy is choosing which risk you can carry
chapters.dek: Not which one has the best backtest. Which tail you can survive, which bleed you can tolerate, and which edge you can actually measure.

figures.title: Run the fund
figures.caption: Unlevered, a dollar in the index becomes $38.80 over thirty years and the tail-hedged index $45.80; put-writing becomes $1.90, because in this model it earns only the premium and the cash securing it earns nothing. At twice the leverage the index fund is closed in year 28, after a crash month lands near its peak, while the tail-hedged fund grows to $924. At three times, all three are closed within seven years. The strategy decides the shape of the returns; the leverage decides whether you survive them.

checks.q: A long-horizon pension and a leveraged hedge fund both consider systematic index put-writing. Who is the more natural seller?
checks.right: The pension, if it can hold through a crash without being forced to sell. The premium pays for bearing a tail; whoever can carry the tail without leverage is the right owner of it
checks.why: The one that can carry the tail. The premium is the same for both; the ability to survive the bad month is not. Leverage converts a drawdown into a forced exit at the worst price, which is why the same strategy can be sensible for one owner and fatal for another.

chapters.text: Four questions sort the playbook for any individual or institution. Which way does your tail point? If a crash would end your business, you should be buying insurance, not selling it, even though insurance loses money on average. If you can survive a crash and hold through it — a pension with a long horizon, a fund with locked-up capital — you may be the natural seller, and you are paid for it. Can you measure the edge? Every strategy here has a measurable premium: implied versus realized, implied versus realized correlation, the event move versus history, the roll yield, the spread net of markouts. If you cannot state yours as a number and track it, you are running the risk without knowing whether you are being paid for it. What does it cost to run? Execution, hedging frequency, financing and borrow can consume a premium that looked generous on paper ( page 13 ). The strategies that look best in backtests are often the ones with the most hidden trading. How big? The same strategy is prudent at one size and ruinous at three times it. Size to the worst plausible month, and use a fraction of Kelly when the edge is an estimate ( toolkit ). Most famous options blow-ups were sound strategies at the wrong size. Choosing is easier to understand from the inside. Run a fund on chapter 01's thirty years: pick a strategy and a leverage, and advance a year at a time. The rule is the one real funds live under: fall 50% from your high and your investors leave. Trader's lens A portfolio manager chooses a strategy and then lives inside its worst month, because that month, not the average, sets how much leverage the fund can carry and whether its investors stay. A strategy with a smooth record and a fat left tail is safe only at the leverage its worst month allows. Size from the worst plausible month, then halve it; the plausible month is never the worst one. Insurance that costs carry in quiet years can be what lets a fund use leverage at all. A drawdown is also a redemption problem: investors leave at the bottom, when the strategy most needs the capital. Rule of thumb: the leverage a strategy can carry is roughly the drawdown you can survive divided by its worst month.
